o: Explain how an operating system manages peripherals and drivers.
Describe user accounts, access rights and file-management functions.
Apply OS functions to school and home scenarios.
c: The OS manages communication between the CPU and peripherals such as printers. A device driver provides software instructions that allow the OS to communicate with the specific hardware.
The OS creates and manages accounts, passwords and permissions; staff and students may be allocated different access rights.
File management means naming, saving, copying, moving, renaming, deleting and organising files within folders/directories.
Device not responding? Consider its driver. A pupil cannot access staff data? Check account rights. Lost a saved document? Locate folders and file paths rather than blaming memory allocation.

m.title: Print through a device driver
m.q: A school printer is installed and students can print from a PC. Explain the role of the operating system and a device driver. [4 marks]
st: Read the sequence: application → operating system → driver → printer.
The OS manages communication with peripherals [1] and processes a print request [1].
A printer driver provides device-specific instructions [1], allowing the computer to communicate correctly with the printer [1].
OS manages peripherals; driver enables communication with particular hardware.

w: A college connects a new digital projector to a teacher's PC. Explain why a suitable driver and peripheral management are needed. [4 marks]

The OS manages communication with the projector [1] as an output peripheral [1]. A suitable driver enables software to send the commands in a format the projector can understand [1], allowing images to be displayed [1].
A pupil account should not modify the school payroll folder. Explain how the OS helps protect files. [4 marks]
The OS uses user accounts [1] to identify the user [1]. Access rights/permissions limit file and folder access [1], preventing pupil accounts from changing payroll files [1].
A pupil saves and moves a homework document into a new subject folder. Describe FOUR file-management operations the OS can provide. [4 marks]
It allows the pupil to name the file [1], save it to storage [1], create/name a folder [1] and move the document into the folder [1].

k.q: Simulate a menu selection choosing a simple file-management action.
k.code:
choice = 2
if choice == 1 then
    print("Save document")
else
    print("Move document")
endif
p: Change choice to 1 and predict again.
Add another output after the condition confirming that the action was selected.
k.a:
Initially: Move document. At choice = 1: Save document.

Extended OCR ERL:
choice = 1
if choice == 1 then
    print("Save document")
else
    print("Move document")
endif
print("Action selected")

Output: Save document, then Action selected.

A hotel has guest and manager accounts on one shared computer. Explain how user management prevents guests from changing booking records. [4 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official past-paper question.
OS assigns different user accounts [1] and can authenticate the person signing in [1]. Access rights restrict guest permissions [1], so only authorised staff can edit booking records [1].

Explain the operating system's roles in file management, device management and user management for a school. [6 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official past-paper question.

It names/saves/moves/organises files [1], allowing pupils to locate work [1]. It manages peripherals/drivers [1] so printers and other hardware can communicate [1]. It manages accounts [1] and access rights to restrict confidential files [1].
v: Software enabling the OS to communicate with a particular device.
Creating, naming, saving, organising and moving files/folders.
Permissions controlling what a user may view or change.
A folder used to organise files and other folders.
x: A device driver helps the operating system communicate with particular hardware.
r: State TWO functions of an operating system. [2 marks]
Provides a user interface [1]; allocates/manages RAM for applications [1]. Other valid functions include file, device, user management and multitasking.
A pupil says a router switches devices on and off. State its real role. [2 marks]
Forwards data between networks [1] using IP addresses [1].
An image is 60 × 20 pixels with 8 bits per pixel. Calculate its raw pixel-data size in bytes. [3 marks]
A colleague claims a two-factor login is unnecessary if a password is long. Explain how two-factor authentication still improves security. [4 marks]
Additional independent evidence is required [1], such as a separate authenticator code/device [1]. A stolen password alone is insufficient [1], reducing unauthorised login risk [1].

priorExam.q: A photographer switches between photo-editing software and a browser. Explain how operating-system memory management and multitasking support this. [4 marks]
priorExam.a: OS allocates RAM to each program [1] so needed data is available [1]. It manages the running tasks and processor time [1], so the user can switch between programs while both remain active [1].
